label: thm:main1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main1}
 Let $f:[0,1)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a bounded $C^1$ monotone function which is non-constant, and let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$. Then the corresponding quasiperiodic family $H(x)$ exhibits a sharp arithmetic spectral transition in frequency for a.e. $x$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}
\item As in \cite{JK2}, the localization part of the conclusion holds for all $x.$
\item
    The $C^1$ assumption in Theorem \ref{thm:main1} is imposed here only for simplicity. The actual hypotheses used in the proof are weaker, and allow points of discontinuity. See Section \ref{sec:ev_branches} and Theorem \ref{thm:monotonederivative_implies_A1A2} for more details; also see Theorem \ref{thm:main2} below.

\item Sharp arithmetic transition in frequency was originally conjectured for the almost Mathieu operator (AMO), $f(x)=2\lambda\cos(2\pi x)$ in \cite{Jit2}.  This conjecture was subsequently established in \cite{AYZ,JL2} (see also \cite{GYZa}), after a sequence of important earlier works \cite{AJ,Jit1, Jit3,LY}. The spectral behavior on the critical line
$|\lambda|=e^{\beta(\alpha)}$ was also investigated in~\cite{AJZ}. 
\item It was conjectured in \cite{JL2} that this sharp transition is universal for one-frequency quasiperiodic operators. It was proved for the Maryland model, $f(x)=\lambda\tan(\pi(x-\tfrac{1}{2}))$, in \cite{JL1,Simon1, HJY}, and for anti-Lipshitz monotone potentials \cite{JK2}. More recently, it was proved for all Type I operators \cite{GJ}, as well as in several other settings \cite{GYZ,HX}, see also \cite{KZ}. As mentioned, quantitative transversality is an important feature of all these families. 

 
\item The absence of point spectrum in $\{E:L(E)<\beta(\alpha)\}$ is actually just a special case of the sharp Gordon-type result of \cite{JK3}, which applies to general functions $f$ of bounded variation. Therefore, we only need to prove the localization part of the result.





\end{enumerate}

label: thm:main2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main2}
    Let $f$ be as in Theorem \ref{thm:main1}. Then there exists for every $\alpha\notin\mathbb{Q}$ some $\eta>0$ depending on $f$ and $\alpha$ such that for every bounded $C^1$ function $g:[0,1)\to\mathbb{R}$, if $|g'(x)|<\eta$ for all $x\in[0,1)$, then the quasiperiodic family associated with $f+g$ exhibits a sharp arithmetic transition.
head: environment

label: thm:main3
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main3}
    Let $f$ be a bounded, monotone, piecewise absolutely continuous function. Suppose that there is some interval $I\subseteq[0,1)$ and $\gamma>0$ such that for almost every $x\in I$, $f'(x)>\gamma$. Suppose in addition that the discontinuities of $f$ do not lie on the same $\alpha$-trajectory. Then $H(x)$ exhibits a sharp arithmetic transition.
head: environment

label: cor
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor}
		For Diophantine $\alpha$ under the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:main3}, if $f$ is non-zero then the Lyapunov exponent $L(E)$ is positive for Lebesgue-almost every $E$ and therefore $H(x)$ almost surely has pure point spectrum with exponentially localized eigenfunctions.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
It is instructive to compare this with the Sturmian case. Fix
an irrational $\alpha\in(0,1)$ with $\beta(\alpha)=0$ and $\lambda>0$,
and consider
\[
 f_0(x)=\lambda\mathbf 1_{[1-\alpha,1)}(x),\qquad x\in[0,1).
\]
The corresponding operators have purely singular continuous spectrum
for every phase~\cite{dkl}. Now replace the increasing jump at
$1-\alpha$ by a smooth monotone transition on an arbitrarily short
interval, keeping the downward jump at $0$, see Figure~\ref{fig:sturmian_comparison}. By
Corollary~\ref{cor}, the resulting operators have Anderson
localization for almost every phase. Thus smoothing just one of the
two jumps changes the almost-sure spectral type, even though the
sampling function still has two flat pieces covering all but an
arbitrarily small part of the circle.\footnote{The statement is for almost every rather than every phase because, theoretically, a zero measure set of phases can have spectral measures partially supported on the (measure zero) set of $E$ with $L(E)=0$ where we do not make any claim. }
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In the context of Theorem~\ref{thm:main2} one does not get all-coupling localization if $f+g$ is non-monotone. The Lyapunov exponent is still positive for Lebesgue-almost every energy by \cite{DK} and therefore one has no absolutely continuous spectrum. However, if one adds a coupling parameter $H(x)=H_0 + \lambda (f+g)$ then the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:main2} themselves are only guaranteed to hold for $\lambda$ close to $1$. In Section~\ref{sec:ev_branches} we also establish a stricter but more quantitative criterion (Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded_implies_A1A2}) which allows the construction of non-monotone sampling functions which for fixed $\alpha$ satisfy the Anti-Lipschitz property for all small enough $\lambda> 0$. This gives, rather surprisingly, \emph{small-coupling} localization using our results. It seems likely that localization also should hold for large coupling or even all couplings, by virtue of positive Lyapunov exponent, but no applicable results seem to exist.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Using our methods, it is not difficult to establish that there also exist unbounded non-monotone potentials for which the sharp arithmetic transition holds. For that reason it makes sense to develop the abstract theory for unbounded sampling functions (see Proposition \ref{prop:main} below), even though we will postpone specific constructions of examples to future work.

Let $\psi:{\mathbb Z}\to{\mathbb C}$ satisfy the eigenvalue equation \eqref{eq:ev}. Fix $\mu>0$ and integer

\end{equation}

label: lemma:mass_estimate_warmup
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:mass_estimate_warmup}
Consider a partition of the integer interval $[0,n-1]$ into two disjoint subsets $G$, $B$. Assume that for every $i\in B$ the sites $\{i-2,i-1, i+1,i+2\} \cap [0,n-1]$ all lie in $G$. 

If $(E, \psi)$ is an eigenvalue-eigenfunction pair of $H_n(x)$ for some $x\in \mathbb{T}$ then
$$\sum_{i\in G} |\psi(i)|^2 \geq \eta \sum_{i\in B} |\psi(i)|^2$$
with the constant $\eta=\frac{1}{2(3+2\lVert f\rVert_\infty)^2}$. This implies
$$\sum_{i\in G} |\psi(i)|^2\geq \frac{\eta}{1+\eta}$$
and
$$\sum_{i\in B} |\psi(i)|^2\leq \frac{1}{1+\eta}.$$
head: environment

label: eq:warmup_recursion
title: Proof
body_md:
We use the abbreviation $a_i= E-f(x+i\alpha)$ with which the eigenvalue equation is rearranged to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:warmup_recursion}
a_{i+1}\psi(i+1)-\psi(i+2)=\psi(i)
\end{equation}
for $i< n-2$. As \begin{align*}
|\psi(i)|^2 &\leq |a_{i+1}\psi(i+1)|^2 + |\psi(i+2)|^2 + 2|a_{i+1}\psi(i+1)\psi(i+2)| \\
&\leq (|a_{i+1}|+1)^2 \max(|\psi(i+1)|^2, |\psi(i+2)|^2)
\end{align*}
we have 
$$\max(|\psi(i+1)|^2, |\psi(i+2)|^2) \geq \frac{1}{(|a_{i+1}|+1)^2} |\psi(i)|^2\geq \tilde{\eta} |\psi(i)|^2$$
with $\tilde{\eta}=\frac{1}{(3+2\lVert f\rVert_\infty)^2}$ where we use that $E\in \sigma(H_n(x))\subset [-2-\lVert f\rVert_\infty, 2+\lVert f\rVert_\infty]$.

If $i\in B$ then by assumption both sites on the left-hand side are in $G$ and at least on one of those \emph{good} sites the eigenfunction $\psi$ has mass comparable to that on $i$. To cover the case when $i$ is at the upper end of the interval one has to use the recursion in the opposite direction to show also
$$\max(|\psi(i-1)|^2, |\psi(i-2)|^2) \geq \frac{1}{(|a_{i-1}|+1)^2} |\psi(i)|^2\geq \tilde{\eta} |\psi(i)|^2$$
again with both sites on the left-hand side in $G$ if $i\in B$.

In conclusion, for every \emph{bad} site $i\in B$ there exists a nearby \emph{good site} $j\in G$ with $|i-j|\leq 2$ such that
$$|\psi(j)|^2\geq \tilde{\eta} |\psi(i)|^2.$$
Summing over $i\in B$ and accounting for the fact that the same $j\in G$ can be produced by at most two different sites in $B$ we conclude
$$2 \sum_{i\in G} |\psi(i)|^2 \geq \tilde{\eta} \sum_{i\in B} |\psi(i)|^2.$$
The remaining inequalities are immediate consequences of $\ell^2$-normalization.

title: Proof

For fixed $x\in (0,1)$ set $G=\{i \in [0,n-1]: x+i\alpha\in \mathsf{A}\}$ and $B=[0,n-1]\setminus G$. By assumption on $\delta$ the sets satisfy the condition of Lemma~\ref{lemma:mass_estimate_warmup} and hence the Hellmann-Feynman formula \eqref{eq:warmup_HF} implies

label: prop:HF_formula
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Hellmann-Feynman

title: Proof
body_md:
Since each $h(y)$ has $n$ simple (and hence isolated) eigenvalues the (absolute) continuity of the eigenvalue curves $E_k$ follows from the (absolute) continuity of $h$ e.g. through the Weyl inequality
$$|E_k(x)-E_k(y)|\leq \|h(x)-h(y)\|.$$
Since there are no eigenvalue-crossings it is a simple consequence of holomorphic functional calculus that the spectral projections onto the $k$-th eigenvalue $P_k$ are also continuous. Similarly, if $h$ is differentiable at $x$ then $P_k$ is also operator-norm-differentiable at $x$. Therefore the eigenvalue functions $E_k(y)$ defined by $P_k(y) h(y)= E_k(y) P_k(y)$ are also continuous respectively differentiable. Choosing any non-trivial pair $(E_k(x), \phi_k(x))$ the eigenvectors $$\psi_k(y)=\frac{P_k(y)\phi_k(x)}{\|P_k(y)\phi_k(x)\|}$$ are well-defined and continuous on a sufficiently small neighborhood $U$ of $x$ and differentiable at $x$. The Hellmann-Feynman formula \eqref{eq:HF} is then a simple consequence of the Leibniz rule applied to 
$$\frac{d}{dx} E_k(x)= \frac{d}{dx} \langle \psi_k(x), h(x)\psi_k(x)\rangle$$
and noting that two of the three resulting terms cancel due to 
$$0=\frac{d}{dx} 1= \frac{d}{dx}\langle \psi_k(x),\psi_k(x)\rangle = \langle \psi'_k(x),\psi_k(x)\rangle + \langle \psi_k(x),\psi'_k(x)\rangle. $$

label: lemma:poisson
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:poisson}
Let \(H\) be a discrete Schrödinger operator on an integer interval containing $[m_1, m_2]$ for some $m_1 < m_2$ with $|m_1-m_2|>1$ and let \(\psi\) solve \(H\psi=E\psi\). Denote by \(H_{(m_1,m_2)}\) the Dirichlet restriction of \(H\) to the finite interval \( (m_1,m_2)=[m_1+1,m_2-1]\) (i.e.\ the finite matrix with Dirichlet boundary conditions at \(m_1\) and \(m_2\)).
Assume
\[
\mathrm{dist}\!\big(E,\sigma(H_{(m_1,m_2)})\big)\;=\;\delta>0.
\]
Then for every \(m\in(m_1,m_2)\) we have 
\[
|\psi(m)| \;\le\; \frac{1}{\delta}\big(|\psi(m_1)| + |\psi(m_2)|\big).
\]
In particular
\[
\max\{|\psi(m_1)|,|\psi(m_2)|\} \;\ge\; \frac{\delta}{2}\,|\psi(m)|.
\]

title: Proof
body_md: This is an immediate consequence of the Poisson formula.

label: lemma:poisson_mass_transfer
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
There exists a uniform constant $L$ such that for every $x\in \mathbb{T}$ the orbit $(x, x+\alpha, x+2\alpha,..., x+L\alpha)$ contains a point of $I$ and $(x, x-\alpha, x-2\alpha,..., x-L\alpha)$ contains a point of $I+\ell \alpha$. Assuming $n$ is large enough there is then for every $i \in [0,n-1]$ an interval $[m_1,m_2]\subset [0,n-1]$ with $\mathrm{dist}(i, [m_1,m_2])\leq L$ and $x+m_1\alpha\in I$.

Write $a_i:=E-f(x+i\alpha)$. Assume $i \in [0,n-L-1]$ then the recurrence for $i+1$ gives
\[
\psi(i)=a_{i+1}\psi(i+1)-\psi(i+2).
\]
As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{proposition:hf_bound_warmup} one obtains $$\max(|\psi(i+1)|^2, |\psi(i+2)|^2) \geq  \frac{1}{(|a_{i+1}|+1)^2} |\psi(i)|^2\geq \tilde{\eta} |\psi(i)|^2$$
with $\tilde\eta:=\frac{1}{(3+2 C)^2}$. By iterating this estimate at most $L$ times we can conclude that for any $i \in [0,n-L-2] $ and $j\in 1,...,L$ one gets
\[
\max\left(|\psi(i+j)|^2,|\psi(i+j+1)|^2\right) \ \geq \tilde\eta^{L}\,|\psi(i)|^2
\]
i.e. out of any two consecutive sites within $L+1$ steps of $i$ at least one must be larger than the right-hand side.

To also treat the upper end of the interval we can instead use the backward recurrence to conclude that for any $i\in [L+1,n-1]$ and $j\in 1,...,L$ one has
\[
\max(|\psi(i-j)|^2,|\psi(i-j-1)|^2) \geq \tilde\eta^{L}\,|\psi(i)|^2.
\]

We conclude that for every $i \notin \mathcal N_{\mathsf{A}}(x)$ there exists an interval $[m_1, m_2]$, $m_2=m_1+\ell$ with $x+m_1\alpha \in I$ and a site $m \in [m_1,m_2]$ with
$$|\psi(m)|^2 \geq \tilde\eta^{L}\,|\psi(i)|^2.$$
If $m_1 < m < m_2$ then by \eqref{eq:E_not_eigenvalue} and Lemma~\ref{lemma:poisson} we have
$$\max\{|\psi(m_1)|^2,|\psi(m_2)|^2\} \;\ge\; \frac{\delta^2}{4}\,|\psi(m)|^2 \geq \frac{\delta^2}{4} \tilde{\eta}^{L}\,|\psi(i)|^2$$
and thus including the edge case $m=m_1$ or $m=m_2$ we have
$$\max\{|\psi(m_1)|^2,|\psi(m_2)|^2\} \;\ge\; \min\left(1,\frac{\delta^2}{4}\right) \tilde{\eta}^{L}\,|\psi(i)|^2.$$
Note that $m_1,m_2\in N_{\mathsf{A}}(x)$ by assumption. Summing this inequality over $i\notin \mathcal N_{\mathsf{A}}(x)$ and accounting for the fact that each index $m$ can be produced by at most $2L$ different $i$ we obtain
\[
2L
\sum_{m\in\mathcal N_{\mathsf{A}}(x)}|\psi(m)|^2 \geq \min\left(1,\frac{\delta^2}{4}\right)  \tilde{\eta}^{L}\sum_{i\notin \mathcal N_{\mathsf{A}}(x)}|\psi(i)|^2
\]
which can be rearranged to \eqref{eq:mass_lowerbound1} using $\ell^2$-normalization of $\psi$.

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If there exists some $x\in \mathsf{A}$ with $\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)=1$ then this means $x+\alpha \in \mathsf{A}$ and since $\mathsf{A}$ is open there exists an interval $I$ with $I\subset (\mathsf{A}-\alpha)\cap \mathsf{A}$. We can then apply Lemma~\ref{lemma:poisson_mass_transfer} with that interval $I$ for every $E$.

Conversely, if all $x\in \mathsf{A}$ have $\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)>1$ then $x \mapsto H_{[1,\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)-1]}(x)$ is piecewise and norm-continuous, therefore the absence of a common eigenvalue implies that there exists for every $E\in \mathbb{R}$ some $\delta>0$ and some interval $I_E \subset \mathsf{A}$ with $\mathrm{dist}(E, \sigma(H_{[1,\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)-1]}(x)))>2\delta$ for every $x\in I_E$. Then one also has $\mathrm{dist}(E', \sigma(H_{[1,\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)-1]}(x)))>\delta$ for every $E'\in (E-\delta, E+\delta)$. As $\sigma(H_n(x))\subset [-2,2+\lVert f\rVert]$ we can by compactness pick finitely many intervals $I_1,...,I_N\subset \mathsf{A}$ such that for every $E \in [-2,2+\lVert f\rVert]$ there exists some interval $I_j \subset \mathsf{A}$ such that $\mathrm{dist}(E, \sigma(H_{[1,\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)-1]}(x)))>\delta$ for every $x\in I_j$. By making each $I_j$ smaller if necessary we may assume $\ell_\mathsf{A}\rvert_{I_j}$ is a constant that we denote $\ell_j$. From Lemma~\ref{lemma:poisson_mass_transfer} and \eqref{eq:mass_lowerbound1} we therefore conclude
$$\sum_{i\in\mathcal N_{\mathsf{A}}(x)}|\psi(i)|^2 \ \ge\  \frac{\eta}{1+\eta}$$
with $\eta = \min_{j=1,...,N}(\eta_{\delta,I_j, \ell_j})$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose an interval $I\subset \mathsf{A} \cap (\mathsf{A} - \alpha)$, then the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lemma:poisson_mass_transfer} hold for this given $I\subset \mathsf{A}$ uniformly in $E$ with $\ell=1$, i.e. \eqref{eq:E_not_eigenvalue} is vacuous. The interval $I$ and the constant $\eta$  are uniform for all absolutely continuous sampling functions with $\lVert f\rVert_\infty \leq C$. For almost every $x$ we then have
$$E_k'(x)=\sum_{i\in \mathcal N_{\mathsf{A}}(x)} |\psi_k(i)|^2\, f'(x+i\alpha) +  \sum_{i\notin \mathcal N_{\mathsf{A}}(x)} |\psi_k(i)|^2\, f'(x+i\alpha) \geq \frac{\eta}{1+\eta}\gamma_+ + \frac{1}{1+\eta}\min(0,\gamma_-).$$
If the sampling function is piecewise absolutely continuous then the eigenvalue curves are also piecewise absolutely continuous. In between endpoints $\beta_j,\beta_{j+1}$ of a monotonicity interval all discontinuities of $E_k(x)$ come from jump discontinuities of $f$ which are assumed to be positive. Therefore we have
		$$E_k(y)- E_k(x) \geq \int_{x}^y E_k'(z) dz \geq \left(\frac{\eta}{1+\eta}\gamma_+ + \frac{1}{1+\eta}\min(0,\gamma_-)\right) (y-x)$$ 
for all $x<y$ within the same monotonicity interval, which gives a strictly positive anti-Lipschitz constant if
$|\gamma_-| < \eta \gamma_+$. 

If the sampling function is monotone but not necessarily piecewise absolutely continuous then the eigenvalue curves $x\mapsto E_k(x)$ are also monotone and hence have distributional derivatives which are positive measures. Hence, one still has a lower bound given by the absolutely continuous part
$$E_k(x)-E_k(y) \geq \int_{y}^x E'_k(z) dz \geq \frac{\eta}{1+\eta}\gamma_+\cdot(x-y).$$

title: Example
body_md:
For some interval $[a,b]\subset [0,1]$ consider the piecewise linear sampling function
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}
0 & \text{ if }x<a\\
v & \text{ if }x>b\\
v \frac{x-a}{b-a} & \text{ if }x\in [a,b]
\end{cases}$$
for some potential value $v>0$.
Let us fix $\mathsf{A}=I=[a,b]$ then by definition of the return time $\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)$ one has for any $x\in I$ that in the trajectory $(x, x+\alpha, ..., x+\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)\alpha)$ precisely $x$ and $x+\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)\alpha$ are in $I$ and the remaining elements are not. Therefore the potential of any finite-size restriction $H_{[1,\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)-1]}(x)$ for $x\in I$ takes exactly two different values $0$ and $v$, i.e. it is a word determined by the quasi-periodic dynamics. 

For such a locally constant potential only finitely many of the Dirichlet restrictions $H_{[1,\ell_\mathsf{A}(x)-1]}(x)$ are actually distinct and we can label them by words in a finite alphabet. Hence it seems quite possible in principle that they could have an accidental eigenvalue coincidence, or maybe even a systematic one if the words satisfy nontrivial combinatorial relations. However, it will turn out the opposite is true! For generic values of $a,b$ the intricate structure of the words actually makes it completely impossible to have a common eigenvalue, one cannot even get an accidental coincidence if one fine-tunes the values of the potentials.

label: def:word_hamiltonian
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:word_hamiltonian}
Let $W$ be a finite set of words in an alphabet $\mathcal{A}$. We say that $W$ has a common Dirichlet eigenvalue if there is an association of numbers $v: \mathcal{A}\to \mathbb{R}$ such that the Dirichlet Hamiltonians 
$$(H_w\psi)(n) = (\Delta\psi)(n) + v(w_n)\psi(n)$$
on $\ell^2[1, \left \lvertw \right \rvert]$ have a common eigenvalue $E$ for all words $w\in W$.
head: environment

label: theorem:nodirichlet
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theorem:nodirichlet}
Assume that no two endpoints $a_0, ..., a_n$ of the intervals $I_0,..., I_n$ are on the same $\alpha$-orbit and that the interval $G=[a_n,a_0)$ has length less than $1-\|\alpha\|$. Then $G=I_0$ has exactly $n+2$ distinct return words $W=\{w_G(x): x\in G\}$ and each word occurs on some sub-interval of $G$ which has positive length. The words $W$ do not have a common Dirichlet eigenvalue.

label: lemma:returntimes
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:returntimes}
Let $\alpha$ be irrational, then the return times $\ell_G$ of an interval $G=[a,b)$ with $|G|<1-\|\alpha\|$ to itself partition $G$ into two or three different intervals with distinct relatively prime return times.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The return times can be written in terms of the continued fraction expansion \cite{Slater1950}. There are two or three return times with the shortest given by the first denominator $r_1 = q_n$ of $\alpha$ such that $\|q_n\alpha\|<|b-a|$. If there are two return times the larger is of the form $r_2 = q_{n+1} - k q_n$ and if there are three then the larger two are of the form $r_2 = q_{n+1} - k q_n$ and $r_3 = q_{n+1} - (k+1) q_n$, hence relatively prime. That the return times partition $G$ into intervals will be proven in more generality later in Lemma~\ref{lemma:connected_component_words} so we omit the proof.

label: lemma:common_eigenvector
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Because all eigenvalues are simple the eigenvalue curves are continuous and  do not intersect. Therefore one has $E=\lambda_k(H(x))$ for some $k$, i.e. it is the $k$-th eigenvalue independent of $x$. Pick any $x$ in $I$ and consider the path $$t\in [0,1]\mapsto h_t= (1-t)H(a) + t H(x)= \Delta_\ell + V(a) + t (V(x)-V(a)).$$ The path $h_t$ also is monotone and has no eigenvalue intersections, moreover $\lambda_k(h_0)= E = \lambda_k(h_1)$. This is only possible if $\lambda_k(h_t)=E$ for all $t$ since $t\to\lambda_k(h_t)$ is monotone. Let now $\psi$ be a normalized eigenvector with $H(a)\psi=E\psi$. By Hellmann-Feynman applied at $t=0$ we conclude $$\langle \psi, (V(x)-V(a))\psi\rangle = \frac{d}{dt} \lambda_k(h_t)\big\rvert_{t=0} = 0$$ for every $x$. In particular, since
$$\langle \psi, (V(x)-V(a))\psi\rangle= \sum_{j=1}^\ell \lvert V_j(x)-V_j(a)\rvert \; \lvert\psi(j)\rvert^2 = 0 $$ we have $\psi(j)=0$ for every $1\leq j \leq \ell$ such that $V_j(x)\neq V_j(a)$, which implies $V(x)\psi=V(a)\psi$ and hence $\psi$ is actually an eigenvector for all $H(x)$.

label: prop:monotone_no_eigenvalue
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Pick any interval $G=[a,b) \subset I$ such that $a,b$ are not on the same $\alpha$-orbit nor on the same $\alpha$-orbit as $0=1$ nor any other of the discontinuity points of $f$.

Assume for a contradiction that $(H_{[1,\ell_G(x)-1]}(x))_{x\in \tilde{G}}$ has a common eigenvalue $E$, then there exists a continuous family of normalized eigenvectors $(\psi_x)_{x\in \tilde{G}}$  with a common eigenvalue $E$. Here we excluded a finite set of discontinuity points $G_0 =G\setminus \tilde{G}$ that we can write as $G_0=\{z_1,...,z_N\}$ with some ordered points $z_1<z_2<...<z_N$. Note that this set is finite, since by Lemma~\ref{lemma:returntimes} $\ell_G(x)$ takes at most three different values $r_1,r_2,r_3$ on at most three distinct subintervals, hence the number of discontinuities is smaller than $N\leq (r_1+r_2+r_3)(1+N_c)$ where $N_c$ is the number of discontinuity points of $f$ on $(0,1)$. On each interval $(z_i, z_{i+1})$ the map $x\in (z_i,z_{i+1})\mapsto H_{[1,\ell_G(x)-1]}(x)$ is continuous and monotone, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:common_eigenvector} we may therefore assume without loss of generality that $\psi_x$ is constant for $x$ inside any interval $(z_i, z_{i+1})$. For any $x\in \tilde{G}$ define the value set $$\mathcal{V}(x)=\{f(x+j\alpha): 1\leq j \leq \ell_G(x)-1\;\;\wedge \;\; \psi_x(j)\neq 0\}$$
as those values of $f$ which are actually sampled by the corresponding eigenvector. The map $x\in (z_i,z_{i+1}) \mapsto \mathcal{V}(x)$ is constant for every $i$, as the final statement of Lemma~\ref{lemma:common_eigenvector} implies that the common eigenvector for the continuity interval vanishes on all sites $j$ such that $x\in (z_i,z_{i+1})\mapsto f(x+j\alpha)$ is not constant. In conclusion, the total value set $\mathcal{V}:= \bigcup_{x\in \tilde{G}}\mathcal{V}(x)$ is a finite set.

Importantly, one has $\psi_x(j)=0$ whenever $f(x+j\alpha)\notin \mathcal{V}$, or equivalently, $$x+j\alpha\notin f^{-1}(\mathcal{V}) =: \Sigma.$$ Hence, whenever $\tilde{f}$ is a sampling function with $f\rvert_{\Sigma}= \tilde{f}\rvert_\Sigma$ then $\{\psi_x\}_{x\in \tilde{G}}$ is also a family of eigenvectors for the associated Hamiltonians $(\tilde{H}_{[1,\ell_G(x)-1]}(x))_{x\in \tilde{G}}$ still with the same common eigenvalue $E$. We will use this to derive a contradiction to Theorem~\ref{theorem:nodirichlet}.

As $f$ is monotone we can write the pre-image of $\mathcal{V}$ as a finite union of disjoint intervals, in particular its closure is
$$\overline{\Sigma} =\bigcup_{i=0}^n [x_i, y_i]$$
with endpoints $0\leq x_0 \leq y_0 \leq x_1 \leq y_1 \leq ... \leq x_n \leq y_n\leq 1$ and then $f$ is constant on the interior of each interval $(x_i,y_i)$ with some value $f\rvert_{(x_i,y_i)}=c_i$. We can pick successively elements $y_{i-1} \leq a_i \leq x_{i}$ such that in the collection $\{a_i\}_{i=1,...,n}$ no two elements are on the same $\alpha$-orbit nor on the same $\alpha$-orbit as $a,b$ or $0=1$. This is always possible since we are picking $a_i$ either from an open interval (if $y_{i-1}<x_i$) or it is fixed to be one of the discontinuity points of $f$ (if $y_{i-1}=x_i$) and those are on distinct $\alpha$-orbits by assumption. In addition we set $a_0=0$ and $a_{n+1}=1$. Setting
$$\tilde{f}(x) = \begin{cases}
f(x) & \text{if }x\in \Sigma\\
c_i & \text{if }x\in [a_i, a_{i+1}) \setminus \Sigma
\end{cases}$$
we obtain a function with $f\rvert_{\Sigma}=\tilde{f}\rvert_{\Sigma}$ and such that the finite-size restrictions $(\tilde{H}_{[1,\ell_G(x)-1]}(x))_{x\in \tilde{G}}$ only sample $\tilde{f}$ on the intervals $\tilde{f}^{-1}(c_i)$ where it is locally constant. Those intervals where $\tilde{f}$ is constant are not necessarily half-open, but the distinction becomes irrelevant if we exclude a countable set: When we set $\hat{G}\subset \tilde{G}$ with $\tilde{G}\setminus \hat{G}$ given by all points on the same $\alpha$-orbit as the endpoints $a_0,...,a_n$ then one obtains
$$\{\tilde{H}_{[1,\ell_G(x)-1]}(x): x\in \hat{G}\}= \{H_w: w\in W\} $$ with Hamiltonians as in Definition~\ref{def:word_hamiltonian} and $W$ a collection of return words of $G$ with respect to a finite family of labeled half-open intervals $(I_j)_{j\in J}$ whose endpoints lie in $\{a_k\}\cup \{a,b\}$. By construction none of these endpoints are on a common $\alpha$-orbit and therefore all return words of $(I_j)_{j\in J}$ occur on subintervals of $G$ of positive length. Therefore $W$ is in fact the collection of \emph{all} possible return words with respect to $(I_j)_{j\in J}$ as the countably many exclusions $G\setminus \hat{G}$ cannot cause us to miss a return word. We conclude that the family having $E$ as a common eigenvalue is a contradiction to  Theorem~\ref{theorem:nodirichlet}.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{proposition:no_common_ev_dirichlet_laplacian}

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:returntimes} the set $W$ has either two elements $W=\{l^{r_1-1}, l^{r_2-1}\}$ or three elements $W=\{l^{r_1-1}, l^{r_2-1}, l^{r_3-1}\}$ where $l$ is the letter associated to $I_1$ and $r_i$ are the return times of $G$ of which there are either two or three distinct ones. Since there is only one letter the Hamiltonians are up to a constant shift the discrete Dirichlet Laplacians on intervals of length $|w|=r_i-1$. Since the return times are relatively prime the eigenvalues of the Dirichlet Laplacians given by solutions of the equations
$$E_k=2\cos\left(\frac{k\pi}{r_i}\right), \qquad k=1,...,r_i-1$$
never have an eigenvalue in common.

label: lemma:stripping
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For the contrapositive let $W_1$ have a common Dirichlet eigenvalue. Then by assumption no word in $W_1$ is empty. Then we can assume an association of values to letters such that for all $w\in W_1$ the Hamiltonians $H_w$ have some common eigenvalue $E$. If $\tilde{w} \in W_1\cap W_2$ is a shared word then any Hamiltonian $H_{\tilde{w}}$ trivially also has eigenvalue $E$. For a new word $\tilde{w}\in W_2\setminus W_1$ we assume $w=\tilde{w}lv$ with the other order being similar. By a simple transfer matrix argument any non-zero Dirichlet eigenvector $\psi$ of $H_w$ with energy $E$ is equal to a Dirichlet eigenvector of $H_v$ when restricted to the final $|v|$ sites and vanishes on the site adjacent to $v$, i.e. the one corresponding to $l$ here. The restriction of $\psi$ to the first $|\tilde{w}|$ letters therefore also satisfies Dirichlet boundary conditions, hence $E$ is also an eigenvalue of $H_{\tilde{w}}$ if $\tilde{w}$ is non-empty. And indeed $\tilde{w}$ cannot be empty, since then the solution $\psi$ would be zero on the first two sites of $w=lv$ due to Dirichlet boundary conditions, hence would have to vanish identically by a transfer matrix argument.

label: lemma:partition
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:partition}
Let $G=[a,b)\subset \mathbb T$ be an interval with $a\neq 0\neq b$, and let $T(x)=x+\alpha \pmod 1$ 
with $\alpha$ irrational. Define
\[
G_1 := T(G), \qquad 
G_{i+1} := T(G_i\setminus G) \quad (i\ge 1).
\]
Let $\ell_G(x)=\min\{n\ge 1 : T^n x\in G\}$ be the first return time to $G$ and
\[
r := \max\{\ell_G(x) : x\in G\}.
\]
Then the sets $G_i$ for $1\le i\le r$ are pairwise disjoint half-open intervals,
$G_i\neq \emptyset$ for $1\le i\le r$, $G_{r+1}=\emptyset$, and
\[
\mathbb T = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^r G_i.
\]

In conclusion, there is for every $x\in \mathbb{T}$ some unique $x_0\in G$ whose orbit meets $x$ before returning to $G$ and the unique index $i$ such that $x\in G_i$ is the time it takes $x_0$ to reach $x$, i.e. $T^i(x_0)=x$.

label: eq:lemma_return_intervals_tech
title: Proof
body_md:
It is clear that all $G_i$ are half-open intervals, since no $G_i$ can be equal to $G$ for irrational $\alpha$, so the operation $G_i\setminus G$ always results in a half-open interval or an empty set.

For $i\ge 1$ define
\[
I_i := T^{-i}(G_i)\subset G,
\]
so that $G_i=T^i(I_i)$. We prove by induction that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:lemma_return_intervals_tech}
I_i
=
\{x\in G : T^k x\notin G \text{ for } k=1,\dots,i-1\}.
\end{equation}
For $i=1$ this is clear since we have $G_1=T(G)$ and hence $I_1=T^{-1}(G_1)=G$. Assume \eqref{eq:lemma_return_intervals_tech} holds for some $i\ge 1$. From the recursion
\[
G_{i+1}=T(G_i\setminus G)=T(T^i(I_i)\setminus G)
\]
applying $T^{-(i+1)}$ gives
\[
I_{i+1}
=
T^{-(i+1)}(G_{i+1})
=
T^{-i}(T^i(I_i)\setminus G)
=
I_i \setminus T^{-i}(G).
\]
Thus $x\in I_{i+1}$ if and only if $x\in I_i$ and $T^i x\notin G$. By the induction hypothesis, this is equivalent to $T^k x\notin G$ for $k=1,\dots,i$.

Using \eqref{eq:lemma_return_intervals_tech} we can now prove that the intervals $G_i$ are disjoint.
Suppose $y\in G_i\cap G_j$ with $i<j$.
Let $x:=T^{-j}y\in I_j\subset G$. Then
\[
T^{j-i}x = T^{-i}y \in T^{-i}(G_i)=I_i\subset G.
\]
Since $1\le j-i\le j-1$, this contradicts \eqref{eq:lemma_return_intervals_tech} for $I_j$.
Hence the sets $G_i$ are pairwise disjoint.

For the fact about the return time, note that $r$ is the smallest positive number such that $I_{r+1}=\emptyset$ and therefore $I_i\neq \emptyset$ for all $i=1,...,r$. Equivalently, one has $G_{r+1}=\emptyset$ and $G_i\neq \emptyset$ for all $i=1,...,r$.

Finally, we prove the sets $G_i$ cover the torus. For any $x\in \mathbb{T}$ there exists some $n$ such that $T^{-n}x\in G$ since $G$ contains an open interval and $\alpha$ is irrational. For the minimal of such $n$ one then has $x\in G_n$.

label: lemma:connected_component_words
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:connected_component_words}
For $0\leq k\leq n$ define $$x_k=a_k-j_k\alpha$$
where $j_k\geq 1$ is the smallest positive integer with the property $a_k-j_k\alpha\in [a_n
,a_0)$.

Assume $|G|<1-\|\alpha\|$, then the points $x_0,\ldots,x_n$ divide the interval $G$ into $n+2$ connected components. On each connected component, $w_G$ is constant. Furthermore, for $x,y\in G$ which are in different connected components, we have $w_G(x)\neq w_G(y)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each $0\leq k\leq n$, the point $x_k$ is the unique point in $G$ whose orbit hits $a_k$ before returning to $G$. Indeed, by the previous lemma the sets $G_i$ form a partition of $\mathbb T$, so every point of $\mathbb T$ has a unique pre-return representative in $G$. Applying this to $a_k$ gives the uniqueness of $x_k$. The $x_k$ are distinct because of the disjoint $\alpha$-orbits. If $|G|>\alpha$ then some return words can be empty, however, the condition $|G|<1-\|\alpha\|$ ensures that there is at most one empty word (either the leftmost or rightmost), hence uniqueness of the return words will still hold. 

We claim that $w_G$ is constant on each connected component of
\[
G\setminus \{x_0,\dots,x_n\}.
\]
Suppose not. Then there exist two points $x,y$ in the same connected component such that
\[
w_G(x)\neq w_G(y).
\]
Let $j$ be the first position at which the two return words differ. Then one of two things happens: Either one of the words has length less than $j$ (so the $j$-th letter disappears) or both words have length at least $j$ (in which case their $j$-th letters are different). As one moves continuously from $x$ to $y$ inside the same connected component, at the moment when this change first occurs, the point $T^j(z)$ must lie on one of the boundary points $a_k$ for some intermediate point $z$. Indeed, the only way a letter can disappear is that the orbit returns to $G$ exactly at that step, and the only way a letter can change is that the orbit crosses from one interval $I_{k-1}$ to the neighboring interval $I_k$, which again can only happen by passing through the common boundary point $a_k$.

But by the uniqueness established above, the only point in $G$ whose orbit hits $a_k$ before returning to $G$ is $x_k$. Hence $z=x_k$, contradicting the fact that $x$ and $y$ lie in the same connected component of
\[
G\setminus \{x_0,\dots,x_n\}.
\]
This proves that $w_G$ is constant on each connected component.

It remains to show that different connected components correspond to different return words. 
First note that the return length can change only at the points $x_0$ and $x_n$, since these are exactly the pre-return representatives of the two endpoints of $G$. Hence the return length is constant on each connected component of $G\setminus\{x_0,x_n\}$. In particular, if two connected components of
$
G\setminus\{x_0,\dots,x_n\}
$
lie in different connected components of
$
G\setminus\{x_0,x_n\},
$
then the corresponding return words have different lengths and therefore are different.

It remains to compare two connected components lying in the same connected component of
$
G\setminus\{x_0,x_n\}.
$
On such an interval, all return words have the same length. For each fixed position $m$ in the word, the $m$-th letter is determined by which interval $I_j$ contains the point $T^m x=x+m\alpha$.
Since $x\mapsto x+m\alpha$ is a translation, the preimage of each interval $I_j$ is again an interval. Therefore, as $x$ moves from left to right, the $m$-th letter can change only by passing from one interval $I_j$ to the next, and in particular it cannot later return to a previous value.

Now let $J_1,J_2$ be two distinct connected components of $G\setminus\{x_0,\dots,x_n\}$ lying in the same connected component of $G\setminus\{x_0,x_n\}$.
Then moving from $J_1$ to $J_2$ one crosses at least one inner boundary point $x_k$ with $1\le k\le n-1$. At such a point, one of the letters changes. By the monotonicity just proved, this change cannot later be undone when crossing further inner boundary points. Hence the return words on $J_1$ and $J_2$ are different.

label: lemma:xk_perturbation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:xk_perturbation}
For $t\in (a_{n-1},a_n)$ consider the word boundaries
$$x_k(t) = a_k(t) - j_k(t)\alpha$$
as in Lemma~\ref{lemma:connected_component_words} with $j_k(t)$ the minimal number such that $x_k(t)\in [a_n(t), a_0(t))=[t,a_0)$. 

For all $s,t\in (y_i,y_{i-1})$ one has
$$x_k(s)=x_k(t),$$
if $k\neq n$ and
$$x_n(t) = x_n(s) + (t-s).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $k=0,...,n$ and any jump discontinuity $t$ of $j_k$ one has
$$j_k(t-\epsilon)< j_k(t+\epsilon)$$
for every small enough $\epsilon>0$ since $j_k(t)$ is monotone increasing with $t$. By definition of $j_k$ one then has
$$a_k(t) - j_k(t-\epsilon)\alpha  = a_n(t)$$
or
$$a_k(t) - j_k(t-\epsilon)\alpha  = a_0$$
since $a_k(t+\epsilon)-j_k(t-\epsilon)\alpha \notin [a_n(t+\epsilon),a_0)$ for every small $\epsilon>0$. For $k=n$ only the second equation has a solution, namely when
$$t - j_k(t-\epsilon)\alpha  = a_0$$
hence $t\in Y$ since $j_k(t-\epsilon)< r$. For $k\neq n$ one has
$$a_k - j_k(t-\epsilon)\alpha  = t$$
or
$$a_k - j_k(t-\epsilon)\alpha  = a_0$$
and only the first equation has a solution, since $a_k$ and $a_0$ are not on the same $\alpha$-orbit. One concludes also $t\in Y$.

We therefore found that since the interval $(y_i,y_{i-1})$ does not intersect $Y$ all $j_k(t)$ are constant inside.

label: lemma:continuity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:continuity}
For $t\in [a_{n-1}, a_n)\setminus Y$ and any $x\in G_t\setminus \{x_0(t),...,x_n(t)\}$ one has
$$w_{G_s}(x)=w_{G_t}(x)$$
for all $s\in [a_{n-1}, a_n)$ with $$|s-t|<  \min_{k=0,...,n} \mathrm{dist}(x,x_k(t)).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any  $x\in G_t\setminus \{x_0(t),...,x_n(t)\}$ we set 
$$\delta :=\min_{k=0,...,n} \mathrm{dist}(x,x_k(t))$$
and note that $(x-\delta, x+\delta)$ is contained entirely inside a single connected component of $G_t\setminus \{x_0(t),...,x_n(t)\}$. 

By Lemma~\ref{lemma:connected_component_words} the $j$-th letter of $w_{G_t}(y)$ is the same for all $y\in (x-\delta, x+\delta)$ and therefore none of the arcs $(x+j\alpha-\delta, x+j\alpha+\delta)$ for $0 < j <\ell_{G_t}(x)$ can contain any of the points $a_k(t)$. Equivalently this is a lower bound for the minimum distance 
$$\min_{k=0,...,n} \;\;\min_{j=1,...,\ell_{G_t}(x)-1} \mathrm{dist}(x+j\alpha, a_k(t))\geq \delta$$
that the return orbit of $x$ has from any of the boundary points $a_k(t)$.

For all $s$ with $|t-s|< \delta$ one therefore has $w_{G_s}(x)=w_{G_t}(x)$ as only the boundary point $a_n(s)$ is different and it moves by the distance $|a_n(s)-a_n(t)|=|t-s|$ which is not enough to change any letter.

label: lemma:wordsconstant
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:wordsconstant}
For any $t,s \in (y_i,y_{i-1})$ with $|G_t|<1-\|\alpha\|$ and $|G_s|<1-\|\alpha\|$ one has $W_s=W_t$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We claim first that the points $x_0(t),...,x_n(t)$ are all distinct from each other for $t\in (y_i,y_{i-1})$ and also distinct from $t$, hence $W_t$ has exactly $n+2$ elements. Indeed, for $j,k\neq n$ this is immediate by the assumption that $a_j$ and $a_k$ have disjoint $\alpha$-orbits. If $$a_j-m\alpha=x_j(t)=x_n(t)=t-l\alpha$$ for some $1\leq m,l\leq r$, then $t=a_j-(m-l)\alpha$, where $-(r-1)\leq m-l\leq r-1$, which contradicts $t\notin Y$.

By Lemma~\ref{lemma:continuity} one can pick for every return word $W_t$ a representative $x\in G_t\setminus \{x_0(t),...,x_n(t)\}$ which yields the same return for $w_{G_s}(x)$ for all $s$ in an open neighborhood of $t$. Taking the intersection over $n+2$ such representatives gives a neighborhood $U$ of $t$ such that $W_s=W_t$ for all $s\in U$, hence $W_t$ is locally constant in $t$.

label: lemma:onewordchanges
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:onewordchanges}
Fix some $y\in Y$ and set $W_{+}=W_{y+\epsilon}$ and $W_{-}=W_{y-\epsilon}$ for any small enough $\epsilon>0$. Then $|W_-\setminus W_+|\leq 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $w\in W_+\setminus W_-$ be a pre-transition word which disappears. For every $t>y$ let $J_t\subset G_t$ be the maximal open interval such that $w_{G_t}(x)=w$ for all $x\in J_t$. The boundary points of $J_t$ are in $\{x_0(t),...,x_n(t)\}$, hence by applying Lemma~\ref{lemma:continuity} to the midpoint of $J_t$ one has $|J_t|\leq 2|t-y|$: if conversely one had $|J_t|>2|t-y|$ then the midpoint of $J_t$ would still represent the same return word and thus $w$ would have to be a return word in $W_{y-\epsilon}$ for some small enough $\epsilon$.

The points $x_0(t),...,x_n(t)$ are mutually distinct for $t>y$ and by Lemma~\ref{lemma:xk_perturbation} only $x_n(t)$ is not constant, therefore there can only be one unique index $k\neq n$ such that $$\lim_{t\to y+} x_n(t) = \lim_{t\to y+}x_k(t).$$
For $|J_t|$ to shrink to $0$ the interval $J_t$ can only be of the form $J_t=(x_k(t), x_n(t))$ for $t\to y+$. As $k$ is unique and $|W_+|=|W_-|=n+2$ we conclude there can be at most one word in $W_+\setminus W_-$ and therefore $W_-\setminus W_+$ also contains at most one element.

label: lemma:wordchangeanatomy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:wordchangeanatomy}
Fix some $y\in Y$ and for any small enough $\epsilon>0$ set $W_{+}=W_{y+\epsilon}$ and $W_{-}=W_{y-\epsilon}$. Then for every word \(\tilde w\in W_-\setminus W_+\) there exist words \(w\in W_+\), \(\tilde v\in W_-\), and a letter \(l\) such that
\[
w=\tilde w\,l\,\tilde v
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
w=\tilde v\,l\,\tilde w.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix \(\varepsilon>0\) so small that $y$ is the only point of $Y$ in $
(y-\varepsilon,y+\varepsilon)$
		and such that the smallest return time of any interval of size $2\varepsilon$ to itself is larger than the maximal return times of the intervals $G^\pm=[y\pm\epsilon, a_0)$ to themselves.

Let \(\tilde w\in W_-\setminus W_+\), and choose \(x\in G^-\) such that
\[
w_{G^-}(x)=\tilde w.
\]
The \(G^-\)-return orbit of \(x\) must intersect $G^-\setminus G^+$, for otherwise $\tilde w$ would define a return word already belonging to \(W_+\). Moreover, the \(G^-\)-return orbit of \(x\) also cannot both start \emph{and} end in $G^-\setminus G^+$ since we assumed via choice of $\varepsilon$ that the return time of any point in $G^-\setminus G^+=[y-\varepsilon,y+\varepsilon)$ to $G^-\setminus G^+$ itself is larger than the return time to $G^-$. Therefore, either the starting point $x$ or the endpoint $x+\ell_{G^-}(x)\alpha $ of the return orbit is in $G^-\setminus G^+$ and the other one is in $G^+$. 

\begin{enumerate}
\item[Case 1:]
\[
x\in G^-\setminus G^+,
\qquad
			x+\ell_{G^-}(x)\alpha \in G^+.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:partition} there exists a unique point \(\tilde{x}\in G^+\) whose orbit meets \(x\) before returning to \(G^+\).
The \(G^+\)-return orbit of \(\tilde{x}\) reaches $x$ after some $j$ steps $x=\tilde{x}+j\alpha$, which is the first and only time it intersects $G^-\setminus G^+$. After that it follows the \(G^-\)-return orbit of \(x\). Hence
\[
w_{G^+}(\tilde{x})=\,\tilde v l \tilde w \in W_+
\]
where $\tilde v:=w_{G^-}(\tilde{x})\in W_-$ and $l$ is the $j$-th letter of $w_{G^+}(\tilde{x})$.
\item[Case 2:]
\[
x\in G^+,
\qquad
\tilde x:=x+\ell_{G^-}(x)\alpha \in G^-\setminus G^+.
\]
This is the same as case 1 except with the roles of $x$ and $\tilde{x}$ exchanged, i.e.
\[
w_{G^+}(x)=\,w_{G^-}(x) l w_{G^-}(\tilde{x}) \in W_+.
\]
\end{enumerate}
In both cases we have produced a word \(w \in W_+\) such that
\[
w=\tilde w\,l\,\tilde v
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
w=\tilde v\,l\,\tilde w
\]
with some word $\tilde{v}\in W_-$. It remains to show that if $\tilde{w}\in W_-\setminus W_+$ then one must have $\tilde{v}\in W_+$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:onewordchanges} the set $W_-\setminus W_+$ contains at most one element, hence it is sufficient to prove that $\tilde{w}\neq \tilde{v}$ are distinct.

As we argued in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:onewordchanges} the maximal interval $J\subset G^-$ that the post-transition word $\tilde{w}\in W_-\setminus W_+$ occurs on has size $|J|\leq 2\varepsilon$, since otherwise it would also be in $W_+$ by continuity. 
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:connected_component_words} the only way for $\tilde{w}$ and $\tilde{v}$ to be equal is for the points $x,\tilde{x}$  that give rise to them to lie in that same connected component $J\subset G^-\setminus \{x_0(G^-),\dots,x_n(G^-)\}$. By the construction above, either $x$ or $\tilde{x}$ is in $G^+$ and the other of the two points is on its $G^+$-return orbit. Since $x,\tilde{x}\in J$ would imply $|x-\tilde{x}|\leq 2\varepsilon$ this produces a contradiction, as by assumption on $\varepsilon$ the first return time of any interval of size $2\varepsilon$ to itself is longer than $\ell_{G^+}(x)$ and $\ell_{G^+}(\tilde{x})$. Hence $\tilde{w}$ and $\tilde{v}$ are distinct, which completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
(of Theorem~\ref{theorem:nodirichlet})
We proceed by induction over $n$. If $n=1$ then all return words are composed of only one letter and Proposition~\ref{proposition:no_common_ev_dirichlet_laplacian} finishes the proof.

		Assume therefore $n\geq 2$ and let us be given $0<a_0<\cdots<a_n<1$ such that no two of these points lie on the same $\alpha$-orbit. For an eventual contradiction we further assume that the return words $W$ of $G=[a_n,a_0)$ with respect to this $(n+1)$-interval configuration have a common Dirichlet eigenvalue. We may assume $|G|<\|\alpha\|$ as otherwise some return word is empty and we rule an empty word as no common Dirichlet eigenvalue. 

		We now increase the size of $G$. Along the path $t\in (a_{n-1},a_n]$ we have the possible finitely many transition points $Y=\{y_1,....,y_M\}$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:wordsconstant} the collection of return words $W_{t}$ is locally constant for $t$ outside $Y$. Pick one representative from each component of $(a_{n-1},a_n)\setminus Y$ and label them so that $a_{n-1}<t_0<\cdots<t_M<a_n$.

Assume $W_{t_{i+1}}$ has a common Dirichlet eigenvalue, which holds for the base case $W_{t_M}=W$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:onewordchanges} and Lemma~\ref{lemma:wordchangeanatomy} one has $|W_{t_i}\setminus W_{t_{i+1}}|\leq 1$ and if there is some word that changes then Lemma~\ref{lemma:stripping} implies that $W_{t_i}$ also has a common Dirichlet eigenvalue. 

Note that in particular $W_{t_{i}}$ cannot contain an empty word as we rule an empty word as no common Dirichlet eigenvalue, which means the lengths of the intervals $G_{t_i}$ stay bounded by $\|\alpha\|$. If there was no contradiction up until $t_0$ then inductively $W_{t_0}$ has a common Dirichlet eigenvalue. 

		It remains to compare $W_{t_0}$ to the return words $\tilde{W}$ of $\tilde{G}=[a_{n-1},a_0)$ with respect to the $n$ intervals with endpoints $a_0,...,a_{n-1}$. As there are no more transition points between $a_{n-1}$ and $t_0$ the interval $\tilde{G}$ must still have length less than $\|\alpha\|$ as the interval with length exactly $\|\alpha\|$ can only occur as a transition point. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:connected_component_words} the collections $\tilde{W}$ and $W_{t_0}$ therefore have exactly $n+1$ respectively $n+2$ elements. There must be at least one word $w\in W_{t_0}\setminus \tilde{W}$ that disappears in the limit of $t\to a_{n-1}$ and precisely as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:onewordchanges} that there is exactly one return word in $W_{t_0}$ whose representing interval shrinks to zero, while the others stay finite. Therefore, $\tilde{W}$ is a subset of $W_{t_0}$, which accordingly inherits the common Dirichlet eigenvalue. However, the induction hypothesis was that for any $n$-interval configuration the collection of return words has no common Dirichlet eigenvalue, which finishes the proof by contradiction.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $E\in\mathbb{R}$ and write $N(x)\coloneqq N_q(x,E)$. Set
\[
D(x)\coloneqq N(x+q\alpha)-N(x),\qquad x\in[0,1).
\]
By shift invariance of Lebesgue measure,
\[
\int_{[0,1)} D(x)\,dx = \int_{[0,1)}\bigl(N(x+q\alpha)-N(x)\bigr)\,dx=0.
\]
		Moreover, $D$ is integer-valued and piecewise constant. Suppose $\{q\alpha\}< \frac{1}{2}$, then $D(x)\leq 1$ as $N$ has at most one positive jump at some $\beta_k$ along the arc $[x,x+q\alpha]$ and at all other discontinuities $N$ only decreases. Conversely, if $\{q\alpha\}> \frac{1}{2}$ then $D(x)\geq -1$. For the average to be $0$ there must hence exist in either case some $x_0\in[0,1)$
such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Dsmall}
|D(x_0)|\le 1,
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
|N(x_0+q\alpha)-N(x_0)|\le 1.
\end{equation}

Combining \eqref{eq:small_qa} \eqref{eq:large_qa} with \eqref{eq:Dsmall}, we obtain that for every $0\le m\le q-1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:orbitbound}
    N(x_0)-7-n_0\le N(x_0+m\alpha)\le N(x_0)+7+n_0.
\end{equation}

Let $\beta_0<\beta_1<\cdots<\beta_{q-1}$ be the reset points defined above and set $\beta_q=\beta_0+1$.
Write $I_j=[\beta_j,\beta_{j+1})$, with indices modulo $q$. Recall that $N|_{(\beta_j,\beta_{j+1})}$ is monotone
decreasing, and when crossing $\beta_{j+1}$ it can increase by at most $1$.

For continued fraction denominators points on the orbit $\mathcal{O}(x_0)=\{x_0+m\alpha:0\le m\le q-1\}$ have maximum gap $2/{q}$ and also $|I_j|\geq 1/{2q}$. Hence for each $j$ we can find
\[
y_j^-\in \mathcal{O}(x_0)\cap (I_{j-4}\cup I_{j-3}\cup I_{j-2}\cup I_{j-1}),
\qquad
y_j^+\in \mathcal{O}(x_0)\cap (I_{j+1}\cup I_{j+2}\cup I_{j+3}\cup I_{j+4}).
\]
Fix $x\in I_j$. Moving from $y_j^-$ to $x$ crosses at most $4$ jump points, hence $N(x)\le N(y_j^-)+4$.
Similarly, moving from $x$ to $y_j^+$ crosses at most $4$ jump points, hence $N(y_j^+)\le N(x)+4$, that is
$N(x)\ge N(y_j^+)-4$. Together with \eqref{eq:orbitbound} this yields
\[
N(x_0)-11-n_0\le N(x)\le N(x_0)+11+n_0,\qquad x\in I_j.
\]
Since $j$ was arbitrary, the same holds for all $x\in[0,1)$, and therefore for all $x,y\in[0,1)$,
\[
|N(x)-N(y)|\le 22+2n_0,
\]
which is precisely \eqref{eq:Nqx-Nqy}. Now, \eqref{eq:discrepancy_dos} follows by applying the triangle inequality to the standard estimate
$$\left|N(E)- \frac{1}{q}\int_{\mathbb T} N_q(x,E)\mathrm{d}x\right|\leq \frac{2}{q}.$$

name: Koksma's Inequality

title: Proof
body_md:
With the empirical eigenvalue distribution
\[
\nu_{n,x}:=\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\delta_{E_j(x)}
\]
and the DOS measure $\nu$ we can conclude from \eqref{eq:JK-3.12} that
\[
\sup_{E\in\mathbb R}
\left|\nu_{n,x}((-\infty,E])-\nu((-\infty,E])\right|
\leq \frac{8|r|}{sq}+\frac{8n_0+200}{q}.
\]
By a limiting argument the same bound holds for open
half-lines. As $\nu_{n,x}$ and $\nu$ are probability measures we conclude the same bound also holds half-lines $[E,\infty)$. As both measures have total mass one,
the bound also holds for upper half-lines.

For nondecreasing functions $g$ the estimate is therefore immediate from the layer-cake representation $$g(E)- a= \int_{a}^b 1_{\{g(E)>e\}} de$$
with $a=g(-\infty)$ and $b=g(\infty)$. As $g$ is increasing $\{E: g(E)>e\}$ is a half-line, hence
$$\left|\int_{\mathbb R}g\,d\nu
-\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}g(E_j(x))\right| \leq (b-a) \left(\frac{8|r|}{sq}+\frac{8n_0+200}{q}\right).$$
For the general case, one can decompose $g=c+ g_+- g_-$ with a constant $c$ and the difference of two nondecreasing functions for which
$$\mathrm{Var}(g) = g_+(\infty)-g_+(-\infty) + g_-(\infty)-g_-(-\infty).$$

title: Proof
body_md:
Define
$$S=\{x\in [0,1): \|H_{n_0}(x)-E\|>B_+^{\log(2+|E|)}-2\}.$$
One has
$$|f(x)-E|\leq \|H_{n_0}(x)-E\|\leq \max_{0\leq j< n_0} |f(x+j\alpha)-E|+2$$
since $f(x)-E$ is a diagonal element of $H_{n_0}(x)-E$. This gives
$$\{|f-E|>B_+^{\log(2+|E|)}-2\}\subset S \subset \bigcup_{j=0}^{n_0-1} \{x: |f(x+j\alpha)-E|>B_+^{\log(2+|E|)}-4\}.$$
If one has $x\notin S$ then the largest and smallest eigenvalue of $H_{n_0}(x)$ respectively must satisfy
$$E_{\mathrm{min}}(x)\geq E-B_+^{\log(2+|E|)}+2, \qquad E_{\mathrm{max}}(x)\leq E+B_+^{\log(2+|E|)}-2.$$
Since the eigenvalues of $H_{n_0}$ are increasing outside $n_0$ of the reset points $\beta_j$, the set $S^c$ is a union of at most $n_0$ intervals. The characteristic functions $\chi_S$ therefore has variation $\|\chi_S\|_{\mathrm{BV}}\leq 2n_0$.

Using the Koksma inequality and \eqref{eq:orbit_discrepancy} we can bound 
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\#\bigl\{0\leq k<n:\,|f(x+k\alpha)-E|>B_+^{\log(2+|E|)}-2\bigr\}\\
&\leq 4(s+|r|)\|\chi_S\|_{\mathrm{BV}}+n|S|\\
&\leq 8n_0(s+|r|)
   +nn_0\bigl|\{x\in[0,1):\,|f(x)-E|>B_+^{\log(2+|E|)}-4\}\bigr|\\
&\leq 8n_0(s+|r|)
   +\frac{nn_0}{\log(2+|E|)\log B_+}
      \int_0^1\log(|f(u)-E|+6)\,du\\
&\leq 8n_0(s+|r|)
   +n\frac{n_0C(f)}{\log B_+}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here we used translation-invariance of the Lebesgue measure and the Markov inequality.
